1.pericope_label: I saw the Lord standing upon the altar: and he said, Smite the lintel of the door, that the posts may shake: and cut them in the head, all of them; and I will slay the last of them with the sword: he that fleeth of them shall not flee away, and he that escapeth of them shall not be delivered. Though they dig into hell, thence shall mine hand take them; though they climb up to heaven, thence will I bring them down:

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the vision at the shrine of the calf-worship with the angel of the presence beside the Lord, and canvasses the philology of the struck ornament before settling on the horns of the altar; Keil and Delitzsch summarise the command as an order to overthrow the building so that the nation is buried beneath the ruins.

Gill places the vision at the altar of burnt offering at Jerusalem, the Lord having removed from between the cherubim as one about to depart; Calvin argues at length that it can have been nowhere but the lawful altar, since appearing at a rival sanctuary would have been an indirect approbation of superstition.

Clarke allows either rival sanctuary, takes the struck part as the timber above the door, and reads the heads as the chief men marked for destruction; Wesley keeps the Jerusalem altar and hears in the vision a possible warning of a coming departure from Judah too.

Henry reads the posture rather than the place, the Lord removed from the mercy-seat to the judgment-seat to avenge the quarrel of his altar and forbid sacrifice, and distinguishes those brought to heaven by grace from those who climb by presumption.

debates.question: At which altar did the prophet see the Lord standing?

positions.position: At the shrine of the calf-worship, the seat of the rival cult.
At one of the two rival sanctuaries, the passage being a continuation of what precedes.
At the altar of burnt offering before the temple at Jerusalem.
Necessarily at the lawful altar and nowhere else, since a vision granted at a profane temple would have approved its superstition.

debates.question: What is the part of the structure that is smitten?

positions.position: Possibly the wreathed capital of the columns, but more safely the ornamented horns of the altar, since no temple building is mentioned.
The timber binding the wall above the door, or the upper part of the door frame.
The cover above the posts, named perhaps from the apples or pomegranates painted there.

debates.question: Who is cut in the head?

positions.position: Either the lintels themselves, or the chief men, priests, prophets and princes.
The priests and rulers, the word that follows meaning the common people rather than posterity.
The king as the lintel and the princes as the posts.

outliers.claim: Observes that the escapes named were in actual fact impossible cases, set forth as though possible in order to cut off every avenue of escape.

themes: I saw the Lord standing upon the altar: and he said, Smite the lintel of the door, that the posts may shake: and cut them in the head, all of them; and I will slay the last of them with the sword: he that fleeth of them shall not flee away, and he that escapeth of them shall not be delivered.
Though they dig into hell, thence shall mine hand take them; though they climb up to heaven, thence will I bring them down:

3.pericope_label: And though they hide themselves in the top of Carmel, I will search and take them out thence; and though they be hid from my sight in the bottom of the sea, thence will I command the serpent, and he shall bite them: And though they go into captivity before their enemies, thence will I command the sword, and it shall slay them: and I will set mine eyes upon them for evil, and not for good. And the Lord God of hosts is he that toucheth the land, and it shall melt, and all that dwell therein shall mourn: and it shall rise up wholly like a flood; and shall be drowned, as by the flood of Egypt. It is he that buildeth his stories in the heaven, and hath founded his troop in the earth; he that calleth for the waters of the sea, and poureth them out upon the face of the earth: The Lord is his name.

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the creature at the bottom of the sea as the water-serpent; Keil and Delitzsch treat the two verses of power as a deliberate strengthening of the threat, describing the Lord of heaven and earth who sends judgments with omnipotent power.

Gill notes the mountain's woods and caves and grounds the impossibility of escape in omniscience joined to omnipotence; Calvin reports the reading that makes the creature a whale, refuses to confine the captivity clause to one historical flight, and reads the touch as a special threatening rather than a general declaration of power.

Clarke calls the whole series metaphorical, hears the earthquake still in the melting, and describes the eye set for evil as a providence turned against those it once served; Wesley makes the creature a crocodile or shark and presses the ease of the judgment, a touch of the finger and the land melting as snow.

debates.question: What is the creature commanded to bite them in the bottom of the sea?

positions.position: The water-serpent.
The crocodile or the shark.
Possibly not a serpent at all but the whale or leviathan, the word bearing that sense elsewhere.

debates.question: Does the going into captivity refer to one particular flight?

positions.position: It may be voluntary flight abroad to escape danger, the flight into Egypt being the instance.
It must be read generally: exile, though called a civil death, would not be the end of evils, the sword pursuing the exiles too.

debates.question: Is the touch that melts the land a general statement of power or a particular threat?

positions.position: A special threatening, the rising and sinking meaning an inundation that leaves no habitation.
A demonstration of omnipotence supporting the threat.

outliers.claim: Rejects as absurd the handling of the parallel psalm that makes it a statement about the unlimited essence of God, insisting its point is that we are always in his sight.

themes: And though they hide themselves in the top of Carmel, I will search and take them out thence; and though they be hid from my sight in the bottom of the sea, thence will I command the serpent, and he shall bite them:
And though they go into captivity before their enemies, thence will I command the sword, and it shall slay them: and I will set mine eyes upon them for evil, and not for good.

And the Lord God of hosts is he that toucheth the land, and it shall melt, and all that dwell therein shall mourn: and it shall rise up wholly like a flood; and shall be drowned, as by the flood of Egypt.

It is he that buildeth his stories in the heaven, and hath founded his troop in the earth; he that calleth for the waters of the sea, and poureth them out upon the face of the earth: The Lord is his name.

7.pericope_label: Are ye not as children of the Ethiopians unto me, O children of Israel? saith the Lord. Have not I brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt? and the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir? Behold, the eyes of the Lord God are upon the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from off the face of the earth; saving that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott turns the comparison into a question whether Israel was safer than a people it despised, and reviews the proposed identifications of the two places of migration, preferring Crete for the first; Keil and Delitzsch read the following verse as the plain repetition of what the opening vision showed symbolically, election proving no deliverance.

Gill presses the likeness of character, Israel blackened by sin and idolatrous as those it compares itself to, and takes the sinful kingdom for the ten tribes; Calvin rejects that reading as strained, holding that nothing more is said than that their condition differs in nothing from the common class of men, and refuses to restrict the sinful kingdom to one nation.

Clarke identifies the peoples by descent and geography and reads the reservation straight, that the race shall not become extinct but be reserved as monuments of justice and finally of mercy; Wesley states the argument plainly, that the deliverance out of Egypt aggravates the sin rather than securing them.

debates.question: In what sense is Israel like the Cushites?

positions.position: In character: blackened by sin and idolatrous, unable to change their course as that nation cannot change its skin.
In standing only: their condition differs in nothing from the common class of men, and the likeness of an unchanged disposition is a strained reading.
In safety: they are asked whether they are better or safer than a people they despised.

debates.question: Is the sinful kingdom Israel alone?

positions.position: Yes, the kingdom of the ten tribes, peculiarly sinful and to be destroyed by the Assyrian.
No, the words are indefinite of all kingdoms, God summoning the whole world to his tribunal.

debates.question: Is the reservation of the house of Jacob a promise?

positions.position: Yes: the race shall not become extinct but be reserved as monuments of justice and finally of mercy.
No: it is irony aimed at their presumption, as though God's hands were tied and he must spare the doubly guilty.

outliers.claim: Collects from the classical writers that the nation compared with Israel was called blameless and honest and reckoned the first to worship the gods and offer sacrifice, which he takes as evidence of their idolatry rather than their piety.

themes: Are ye not as children of the Ethiopians unto me, O children of Israel? saith the Lord. Have not I brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt? and the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir?
Behold, the eyes of the Lord God are upon the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from off the face of the earth; saving that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob, saith the Lord.

9.pericope_label: For, lo, I will command, and I will sift the house of Israel among all nations, like as corn is sifted in a sieve, yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth. All the sinners of my people shall die by the sword, which say, The evil shall not overtake nor prevent us.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch supply the frame the passage needs, that because the unchangeable One cannot abolish his purpose of salvation the destruction of the sinful kingdom is followed by the setting up of the genuine kingdom of God.

Gill hears in the command only that trying dispensations come by God's appointment and are overruled for his glory; Calvin uses the sifting to prove the previous reservation ironical, denies that any solid grain remained in the body of the nation, derives the disputed word from a root meaning to bind, and makes security itself the chief mark of impiety.

Clarke reads the shaking as a dispersion so ordered that not one grain, however little or contemptible, is lost before a general restoration, and warns that presumptuous fearlessness is no evidence of safety; Wesley says the smallest good grain shall not be lost, and puts the sinners' boast in their own mouths.

debates.question: What is the thing that shall not fall to the earth?

positions.position: A little stone, pebble or gravel: not one of them, however contemptible, is left behind.
The solid grain, the word coming from a root meaning to tie or bind together.
The smallest good grain, preserved through the tossing.

debates.question: Does the sifting promise preservation or completeness of judgment?

positions.position: Preservation: the good are not lost though scattered, and a general restoration follows.
Completeness: the floor is cleansed and nothing remains on it, the body of the nation having become chaff.

outliers.claim: Answers the objection that godly men went into exile by saying that on the threshing floor the wheat is beaten and winnowed together with the chaff and no difference can be observed, God keeping his own gathered in the sieve in a hidden manner.

themes: For, lo, I will command, and I will sift the house of Israel among all nations, like as corn is sifted in a sieve, yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth.
All the sinners of my people shall die by the sword, which say, The evil shall not overtake nor prevent us.

11.pericope_label: In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof; and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old: That they may possess the remnant of Edom, and of all the heathen, which are called by my name, saith the Lord that doeth this.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch mark the structure of the promise, the outward extension of the kingdom here and its inward glorification in what follows.

Gill dates the raising to the gospel age and reports the older Jewish teachers referring the prophecy to the Messiah, one of his names being drawn from this verse; Calvin fastens on the figure of a tabernacle as a mean cottage unfitting royal dignity, and notes that the prophet named David rather than Jesse because that name was in repute.

Clarke argues negatively that no past restoration answers to the terms of the prediction, so that it remains to be fulfilled, and reports then refuses a textual emendation in the following verse; Wesley keeps the literal return from captivity together with the prophecy of the Messiah's kingdom and the bringing in of the Gentiles.

Henry treats the meanness of the tabernacle as the church's standing condition, dwelling as in shepherds' tents to feed and soldiers' tents to fight, and takes the enlargement as the accession of whole countries.

debates.question: When is the fallen tabernacle raised?

positions.position: At the return from captivity and the re-establishment of David's house.
In the gospel age, the older Jewish teachers themselves referring the prophecy to the Messiah.
Not in any past restoration, since neither the respite before the Babylonian captivity nor the later victories answer to the terms; it remains to be fulfilled.

debates.question: Should the text be emended to read that the residue of men may seek the Lord?

positions.position: No: though the Arabic, some Syriac copies and the citation in the New Testament support it, no collated manuscript countenances the change, and the Hebrew must stand.
The received text stands, the possession being understood as the conversion of the remnant according to the election of grace.

outliers.claim: Draws from the raising the general rule that while the world stands God will have a church in it, and if it be fallen down in one place it shall be raised up elsewhere.

themes: In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof; and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old:
That they may possess the remnant of Edom, and of all the heathen, which are called by my name, saith the Lord that doeth this.

13.pericope_label: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes him that soweth seed; and the mountains shall drop sweet wine, and all the hills shall melt. And I will bring again the captivity of my people of Israel, and they shall build the waste cities, and inhabit them; and they shall plant vineyards, and drink the wine thereof; they shall also make gardens, and eat the fruit of them. And I will plant them upon their land, and they shall no more be pulled up out of their land which I have given them, saith the Lord thy God.

schools.summary: Ellicott notes only how rapidly the harvest follows the ploughing and that these closing verses foreshadow the restored kingdom, in which he sees the germ of the later prophecies of the Messiah; Keil and Delitzsch set out the order of the promises, the blessing of the land, then of the nation, then the eternal duration of the kingdom.

Gill denies that the return from Babylon can be meant, since those restored were dispossessed again, and takes the captivity to be the still unended one of Judah and Israel together; Calvin defends the metaphorical manner as an accommodation to a rude people, calls the flowing mountains frank hyperbole, and finds the fulfilment in the spread of Christ's kingdom rather than in any territorial rule.

Clarke keeps the seasons in their natural order and supports the overlapping labours from travellers' reports of the agricultural year, then argues from the failure of every past restoration that the planting must still be fulfilled; Wesley saves the promise by a tacit condition, the sins of the returned captives having prevented the blessings.

debates.question: Why did the promised plenty never appear?

positions.position: The sins of the returned captives prevented it; the blessings were promised under a tacit condition.
It was never meant of territorial plenty: the promise is fulfilled in the spread of Christ's kingdom, and the abundance is spiritual.
It has simply not been fulfilled yet, and because the word of God cannot fail it must be fulfilled hereafter.

debates.question: Is the ploughman overtaking the reaper a natural or a figurative picture?

positions.position: Natural in its detail, the agricultural seasons genuinely overlapping in those countries, though the intent is a poetical image of happy times.
Figurative throughout, borrowed from a blessing in the law, and the flowing mountains sheer hyperbole.

outliers.claim: Rests the certainty of the promise on the closing formula itself: he can do it because he is Jehovah, and he will do it because he is thy God.

themes: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes him that soweth seed; and the mountains shall drop sweet wine, and all the hills shall melt.

And I will bring again the captivity of my people of Israel, and they shall build the waste cities, and inhabit them; and they shall plant vineyards, and drink the wine thereof; they shall also make gardens, and eat the fruit of them.
And I will plant them upon their land, and they shall no more be pulled up out of their land which I have given them, saith the Lord thy God.
